extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and worldbuilders (especially fantasy & science fiction authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for designing and describing geography and biomes in fiction: choosing what the landscape must accomplish for the story, building plausible ecosystems and transitions, and using sensory detail and real-world observation to make settings feel authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-driven geography
rubrics_metrics.description: “What do I need the geography to do?” — design geography to serve story needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the geography should produce sense of wonder, pose a mystery, enable particular plot mechanics, or explain political/economic conditions. Example: a desert planet with an atmosphere that mysteriously exists becomes a central puzzle; a dense atmosphere can allow characters to fly on muscle power for middle-grade fun. The required story effect dictates which geographic features and details you emphasize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the familiar
rubrics_metrics.description: “Start with the familiar, with components that you know really well.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real, personally known places and experiences as a base to gain authenticity and immersive detail; then tweak or extrapolate for fictional settings. Mahtab’s advice: begin with what you can vividly imagine (sights, sounds, smells, tastes, feels) and only later move to invented geographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dig into ramifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When you choose a geographic feature, follow its consequences for culture, politics, economy, and daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how features affect war, religion, resources, settlement patterns, and customs. Example: a religious lake can be the focal point of multi-generational conflict and shape whether communities fish it or forbid access. Spin out ramifications (who uses it, who is excluded, how laws and habits form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use biomes as shorthand for ecosystems
rubrics_metrics.description: “Biomes can help you build a world. Biomes are kind of packaged ecosystems.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in terms like desert, tundra, jungle, forest to simplify ecological thinking and populate landscapes plausibly. Biomes give you ready expectations (flora, fauna, climate) to build from, but you can and should adapt them to fit your story’s needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to transitions and hybrids
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t place biomes as isolated blocks; include gradual transitions and hybrid zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional areas (foothills, saltmarshes near deserts, ecotones) are common in nature and often produce interesting, unique resources or cultural niches. These zones can be rich sources of plot, character, and ecological detail—avoid simplistic 'snow planet/desert planet' binaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: The map is not the territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps are abstractions; real landscapes are three-dimensional, experiential, and often different in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go observe real places when possible. Translate flat map features into sightlines, slopes, footing, and sensory reality. Example: whiteboard or map planning will change when you consider actual terrain, sightlines, and how characters move through space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multisensory description (beyond sight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe landscapes using senses other than sight: sound, smell, taste, and touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise/homework: write a setting with sight removed—how would a blind person describe it? Relying on non-visual senses makes settings more immersive and reveals details sight-based prose misses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tune physical parameters to narrative needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust gravity, atmospheric density, chemistry, and other physical variables to create desired story effects, while considering plausible consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want low gravity or dense air to allow flight, think through side effects (e.g., narcotic atmosphere) and either incorporate them or provide narrative workarounds. Consult experts when necessary to keep internal plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography shapes language and place names
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape features influence vocabulary and toponyms (e.g., Arabic 'wadi' for dry riverbed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect how local geography would plausibly affect language, place-naming, and cultural reference points to add realism and depth (linguistic realism tied to environment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider terrain’s effects on warfare and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Terrain determines what military formations and tactics succeed (e.g., legion vs. phalanx advantages on hills or rough ground).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building geopolitical conflict, match warfare styles and political boundaries to the landscape. Include how mobility, sightlines, and ground conditions favor or hinder certain forces to make conflicts believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on genre tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize common influences (medieval European fantasy, Star Wars-style single-biome planets) and avoid lazy one-note worlds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more complex, mixed, and regionally-specific features instead of defaulting to stock settings. Diversify your biomes and transitions to create originality and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research unfamiliar or scientifically different settings
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating settings unlike your lived experience (e.g., Mars, exotic ecosystems), do research and consult domain experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest effort to learn the real-world science or comparable analogues so invented details are convincing. Research enriches texture and helps you foresee plausible ramifications of geographic choices.
